# Vendored code

## shavar.js

Verbatim copy of `js/shavar.js` from the sibling **shavar** project.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Source repo | `../shavar` (local sibling of this repo) |
| Source path | `js/shavar.js` |
| Upstream commit | `2482824bd7b705cc5bc58a5c660d75a8cad1e840` |
| SHA-256 of the copy | `ab5b928727808d04f3224861b50516ac79290fec61ecdc1e206f4640de0a8e9c` |
| Retrieved | 2026-08-09 |

**Do not edit this file.** It is copied byte-for-byte so that it can be
re-synced from upstream with `cp`, and so that `shatool` inherits upstream's
test coverage (1154 NIST CAVP vectors, cross-checked against six other
implementations) without re-deriving it. `tests/run.js` re-verifies the copy's
checksum and runs its built-in `selftest()` on every run, so a silent
divergence between the two repos fails the build here.

To re-sync:

```sh
cp ../shavar/js/shavar.js js/vendor/shavar.js
# then update the commit and checksum above, and EXPECTED_SHAVAR_SHA256 in
# tests/run.js
```

### Why this library

It exposes the SHA-256 interior rather than just a digest: `traceBlock()`
returns the complete per-round record (`W`, `A`, `E`, `T1`, `T2`) for a chosen
block, which is precisely what this tool visualizes. It also supports
arbitrary **bit** lengths — not just whole bytes — which is what makes the
default 513-bit input expressible at all.

It defines a single frozen global, `SHAVAR`, with no `import`/`require`, so it
loads as a classic `<script>` from a `file://` URL. This repo follows the same
convention for the same reason; see `NOTES.md`.
